comments.text:
1. Narashansah (नराशंस)
Found in all four Vedas (including the Rigveda and Atharvaveda), this is the most widely discussed name.
Meaning: The word is a combination of Nara (man) and Ashansah (praised). Thus, it means "The Praised One."
Connection: This is the literal translation of the Arabic name Muhammad.
Context: In the Kuntap Suktas (Atharvaveda 20.127.1), Narashansah is described as a "camel-riding Rishi" who is protected from 60,090 enemies, which scholars correlate to the Prophet's life and the population of Makkah at the time.

2. Mahamad (महामद)
This name appears directly in the Bhavishya Purana (Prati Sarg Parv III, Khand 3, Adhyay 3, Shlokas 5-8).
Context: The text mentions a "Mleccha" (foreigner) spiritual teacher named Mahamad who will appear in a desert land (Arabia) with his companions.
Description: He is described as a reformer who will establish a new religion, be circumcised, keep a beard, and call people to prayer.
Note: Traditional Hindu scholars often interpret these verses differently, sometimes viewing the figure in a historical context related to the arrival of Islam in India, rather than as a divine prophecy.

3. Kalki Avatar (कल्कि अवतार)
Many researchers argue that the description of the Kalki Avatar (the final avatar of Vishnu) in the Kalki Purana matches Prophet Muhammad.
Parental Names: The scripture says Kalki's father will be Vishnuyash ("Servant of God") and his mother Sumati ("Peaceful/Pure"). In Arabic, Muhammad’s father was Abdullah (Servant of Allah) and his mother was Aminah (Peaceful).
Location: Kalki is prophesied to be born in Shambala, which some interpret as "the land of peace," a title often associated with Makkah.
Attributes: Kalki is described as riding a white horse and carrying a sword to fight evil, which mirrors the era and methods of the Prophet.

4. Ahmad (अहमद)
Some interpretations of the Sama Veda (II:6, 8) suggest the presence of the name Ahmad.
Context: This is another name for Prophet Muhammad (meaning "one who praises"). Certain mantras mention a teacher receiving wisdom or "eternal law" from his Lord, which some scholars link to the revelation of the Quran.
